title: The first battle
carry: sthitaprajna: wisdom that stands still in the noise
last: RAMA TURNS AWAY NO ONE WHO ASKS REFUGE.

cards: Some nights the noise doesn't stop. The neighbors are fighting, the baby won't sleep, your phone keeps lighting up, your own head won't quiet down. Lanka, now, is that loud.
A golden city on a mountain, ringed with walls and moats, four great gates, each guarded by an army. Outside, on the plain, a sea of monkeys and bears, and two princes with bows. The talking is over.
Angada's embassy failed. Vibhishana has told Rama where every gate is. At dawn, the monkeys rush the walls, climbing, hurling rocks and trees.
And the fighting doesn't stop when the sun goes down.

teach.h: THE FIGHTING RUNS INTO THE NIGHT.
teach.b: Valmiki's war books are long, loud and crowded. Duel after duel: monkey against demon, champion against champion, names you'll never need to remember.
The first day's fighting runs into the night, and that's when it gets frightening. The demons of Lanka are said to grow stronger in the dark. Nobody can see who's friend and who's enemy.
Valmiki describes a terrible darkness filled with shouting, the clash of weapons, cries in the dark, rivers of blood. The monkeys lash out at shadows; some fight their own side by mistake.

And in the middle of the chaos, the story keeps putting one image in front of us: Rama, steady. Arrows come from every side, and he answers them calmly, one at a time, as if the noise isn't touching him.
Under the story runs a second one. A battle isn't only outside.

teach.h: IN THE DARK, SWINGING AT SHADOWS.
teach.b: The noise gets in, the fear gets in, the confusion gets in, and you start swinging at shadows.
The Bhagavad Gita, the book you met on day twenty-one, has a word for the person who stays level in pleasure and pain, in noise and quiet: sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands still.

teach.h: RAMA, STEADY, ONE ARROW AT A TIME.
teach.b: Many teachers read Rama, in this scene, as a picture of that, and Hindus are taught to aim for it themselves. Not someone who's escaped the fight.

Someone in the middle of it, still inside. The walls of Lanka won't fall for a long time; this is the first night of many. And already the question is not only who wins, but who can stay steady until morning.

how: The war in Lanka is staged over several nights in the Ramlila plays of north India that lead up to Dussehra; some readers take the battle both as a story and as a picture of the inner struggle to stay steady.

o: a sage who has left the world behind for silence
a warrior who simply never feels any fear
one whose wisdom stays steady in noise and pain

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a golden city with four gates
told Rama where every gate was
friend and enemy lost in the dark
the one whose wisdom stands still

s: the first battle ended at sunset
it ran on into the night, the most frightening part.
in the dark, some monkeys fought their own side
Valmiki describes confusion so deep that friend and enemy couldn't be told apart.
sthitaprajna is a word from the Gita
it names the one who stays steady in pleasure and pain.

games.q: you're in the night battle. it's pitch dark, shouting everywhere, and something moves beside you. what do you do?
o: stop, and look before you strike.
games.why: in the story, the monkeys who swung at shadows sometimes hit their own side. the image the story holds up instead is Rama, steady, one arrow at a time.

practice: Don't try to make it quiet: let whatever noise is around you, traffic, voices, a hum, a fan, be there, and find your breath underneath it.
Each time a sound grabs you, or your own mind is the noisy one, notice it and come back to one breath. You're not winning against the noise; you're staying level in it.

wordCard.voice: Sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands still in pleasure and pain. Lanka's first battle runs into the dark, and one warrior stays steady inside it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Lanka, Ravana's island city, built on a mountain across the sea.

carryVoice: Your line: sthitaprajna, wisdom that stands still in the noise. The first night in Lanka is long. Steady, till tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (the siege of Lanka; the night battle, roughly sargas 41–44)
